title: The Turnip Trouble in Oakhaven
markdown:
In Oakhaven a brook babbled as if it had opinions, and rolling hills threw gentle shadows across plots that believed in vegetables. Basil Green lived there with soil on his tweed and flour on his cuffs, spectacles bobbing on the tip of his nose whenever he spoke of shared work. He was a socialist in the enthusiastic, disorganized sense: communal baking, community gardens, the conviction that the village could, if it pulled together, produce both decent bread and a better world. His jacket never quite recovered from either project.

Lady Honoria Pumble oversaw the countryside with hats as carefully composed as her public image. Gowns at village events shimmered like dragonfly wings. Her smile, a practised blend of warmth and regal grace, could unthaw a frost. She loved Oakhaven. She also loved the gasps that followed her announcements of fountains, painted hall-signs, and other improvements best unveiled with a flourish. Charity, for Lady Honoria, was an art with an audience.

One bright spring Basil declared, at market, that Oakhaven would embrace the humble turnip. “To the soil, comrades!” The chickens scattered, which he took as revolutionary energy. “We will grow the finest roots this shire has seen, and share them. No family hoards the plumpest.” The plan had volume. It did not, as yet, have a blueprint.

Lady Honoria heard the volume and saw a festival. “My dear Mr. Green,” she said at the next gathering, voice like silver bells, “your sentiment is admirable. A grand event would celebrate our collective harvest. I shall sponsor the first Great Oakhaven Turnip Festival. The best grower wins a gleaming silver trowel and a year’s finest seed.” Villagers cheered, already polishing imaginary silver. Basil, annoyed that personal glory had parked itself on his collective dream, could not deny the excitement. His idealism had been hijacked by bunting. He told himself bunting could still feed people.

Summer thickened. Then a creeping grey fuzz appeared on the broad green leaves. Turnips that had promised plumpness began to shrivel. Green went brown. Despair settled over a village that had already ordered extra cream for the festival. Basil had named his prize specimen Radical Reginald, with the sincerity of a man who believed names conferred character. He watched Radical Reginald droop, and felt his own speeches droop with it. Lady Honoria’s marquees suddenly looked like tents for a wake.

Old Mrs. Higgins, who had been watching the blight with the patience of someone who had told the village things before, hobbled forward. “Not common blight,” she croaked, voice like dry leaves. “Grumbling Grubs. They thrive when the soil is too sour. It needs lime. I’ve said for years the ground by the old quarry is grumpy.” Lady Honoria, busy with music and bunting, blinked. Soil was not a social event. Basil felt the familiar inadequacy: passion had not budgeted for acidity.

Among wilting greens he did something that surprised him. He swallowed the pride that made aristocratic patronage look like a trap, and walked not to Radical Reginald but to Lady Honoria, who was dabbing a theatrical tear with lace. “Lady Honoria. Mrs. Higgins is right. The soil is the problem. Your festival has brought us together. Perhaps we use that for something practical.”

She looked at him, genuine surprise replacing practised benevolence. “You mean, instead of judging grown turnips, we help them grow?”

“You have resources. We have villagers who now understand why nothing is growing. If you secure the lime, I will show them how to put it down.”

The alliance was unlikely and, for that reason, useful. Lady Honoria rallied staff and suppliers with the same flourish she used for fountains, only this time the flourish delivered bags. Agricultural lime appeared, smelling faintly of earth and invoices. Basil shed his market roar for a quieter intensity and went plot to plot along the quarry edge: how much, how to mix, how to spread without sulking at the soil. Villagers who had come for speeches stayed for trowels. The grey fuzz receded like a rumour that had been out-argued. Leaves unfurled. Radical Reginald, traitor to tragedy, swelled with unideological roundness, and Basil, who had been prepared to eulogise him, found himself instead advising Daisy Meadowsweet on drainage.

The Great Oakhaven Turnip Festival, when it arrived, was a display of healthy roots rather than a monument to disappointment. Marquees that had looked like wake-tents now smelled of earth and tea. The silver trowel went to young Daisy Meadowsweet for a specimen that needed no speech, only a clean cut and a modest blush. Villagers who had been recipients of charity or followers of slogans felt, instead, the ordinary thrill of having solved a problem with lime under their nails. Someone had even remembered Mrs. Higgins in the programme, in small type, which she pretended not to notice.

Basil stood a little aside, less a voice of pure theory than a man who had asked for help and given instructions that worked. Lady Honoria, for once, found a warmth that did not require applause: the glow of a village that had grown something together, including, inconveniently, a little respect.
characters: Basil Green (village socialist), Lady Honoria Pumble (benevolent landlord)
